'''Lawrence Sims Bartell''' (23 February 1923, [[Ann Arbor]], [[Michigan]] – 8 September 2017, Ann Arbor) was the [[Philip J. Elving]] [[emeritus|Professor Emeritus]] of Chemistry at the [[University of Michigan]]. His research in [[physical chemistry]] focused on [[electron diffraction]] studies of molecular structure and later on [[molecular mechanics]]. Bartell retired from his faculty position at Michigan in 1993.<ref name="umich">{{cite web|title=Memoir: Lawrence S. Bartell|url=http://um2017.org/faculty-history/faculty/lawrence-s-bartell/memoir|website=University of Michigan Faculty History Project|accessdate=10 March 2017|date=1 December 1993}}</ref>

==Early life and education==
Bartell was born on February 23, 1923, in [[Ann Arbor, Michigan]], the son of noted University of Michigan chemistry professor [[Floyd Bartell]]. The younger Bartell briefly attended the [[University of North Carolina]] as an undergraduate before returning to complete his studies at the University of Michigan, from which he received his B.S. in 1944.<ref name="bn">{{cite journal|last1=Kuczkowski|first1=R.L.|title=Lawrence S. Bartell: biographical notes|journal=Journal of Molecular Structure|date=August 1999|volume=485-486|issue=1–3|pages=xi–xxvii|doi=10.1016/S0022-2860(99)00037-X|bibcode=1999JMoSt.485D..11K}}</ref> As he later recalled, before he had finished his studies he was invited by [[Glenn Seaborg]] to interview for a position working on the [[Manhattan Project]]. He accepted the job and worked on methods for extracting [[plutonium]] from [[uranium]]. He was subsequently drafted into the Navy and served for nine months before being discharged for disability due to [[rheumatic fever]].<ref name="ahf">{{cite web|title=Lawrence Bartell|url=http://www.atomicheritage.org/profile/lawrence-bartell|website=Atomic Heritage Foundation|accessdate=10 March 2017}}</ref><ref name="kelly">{{cite web|last1=Kelly|first1=Cindy|title=Lawrence Bartell's Interview|url=http://manhattanprojectvoices.org/oral-histories/lawrence-bartells-interview|website=Manhattan Project Voices|accessdate=10 March 2017|date=9 May 2013}}</ref> He subsequently returned to the University of Michigan and received his Ph.D. in 1953 under the supervision of [[Lawrence Brockway]].<ref name=umich /><ref name="hargittai">{{cite book|last1=Hargittai|first1=István|last2=Hargittai|first2=Magdolna|title=Candid Science III: More Conversations with Famous Chemists|date=2003|publisher=World Scientific|isbn=9781783261116|chapter=5: Lawrence S. Bartell}}</ref>

==Academic career==
Bartell began his academic career at [[Iowa State University]], where he joined the faculty in 1953. He moved to the University of Michigan in 1965,<ref name=bn /> where he would remain until his retirement in 1993. He was named the [[Philip J. Elving]] Professor of Chemistry in 1987. Bartell chaired the Division of [[chemical physics|Chemical Physics]] of the [[American Physical Society]] from 1977 to 1978 and served on the [[editorial board]]s of several [[scientific journal]]s specializing in chemical physics.<ref name=umich /><ref name=bn /> A type of [[electron microscope]] used by his research group was noted by the ''[[Guinness Book of World Records]]'' in the 1970s as most powerful in the world at the time.<ref name=kelly /><ref name=bn />

After his retirement, Bartell has written several [[memoir]]s, including a paper describing his experiences working on the Manhattan Project<ref name="mp">{{cite arXiv|title=Work on the Manhattan Project, Subsequent Events, and Little Known Facts Related to its Use|eprint=0911.4088|date=20 November 2009|last1=Bartell|first1=Lawrence S|class=physics.hist-ph}}</ref> and a self-published book called ''True Stories of Strange Events and Odd People: A Memoir''.<ref name="stories">{{cite book|last1=Bartell|first1=Lawrence S.|title=True Stories of Strange Events and Odd People A Memoir.|date=2014|publisher=Iuniverse Inc|isbn=978-1491720219}}</ref> Bartell died in September 2017.<ref name=obit>{{Cite web|url=http://obits.mlive.com/obituaries/annarbor/obituary.aspx?pid=186649769|title=Obituary: Lawrence Bartell|date=14 September 2017|website=Ann Arbor News|access-date=25 October 2017}}</ref>

==Awards and honors==
* Fellow, [[American Physical Society]], 1968<ref name="aps">{{cite web|title=Fellow Archive|url=https://www.aps.org/programs/honors/fellowships/archive-all.cfm?initial=&year=1968&unit_id=DCP&institution=|website=American Physical Society|accessdate=9 March 2017}}</ref>
* University of Michigan Distinguished Faculty Achievement Award, 1981<ref name=umich />
* Michigan Association Governing Boards Distinguished Faculty Award, 1982<ref name=umich />
* National Science Foundation Creativity Award, 1982<ref name=umich />
* Michigan Scientist of the Year, 1986<ref name=umich />
